A Reduction from Delayed to Immediate Feedback for Online Convex Optimization with Improved Guarantees

Alexander Ryabchenko 1 2  Idan Attias 3  Daniel M. Roy 1 2 

††footnotetext: 1University of Toronto 2Vector Institute 3Institute for Data, Econometrics, Algorithms, and Learning (IDEAL), hosted by UIC and TTIC. Correspondence to: Alexander Ryabchenko <alex.rbch.research@gmail.com>, Idan Attias <idanattias88@gmail.com>, Daniel M. Roy <daniel.roy@utoronto.ca>.
Abstract

We develop a reduction-based framework for online learning with delayed feedback that recovers and improves upon existing results for both first-order and bandit convex optimization. Our approach introduces a continuous-time model under which regret decomposes into a delay-independent learning term and a delay-induced drift term, yielding a delay-adaptive reduction that converts any algorithm for online linear optimization into one that handles round-dependent delays. For bandit convex optimization, we significantly improve existing regret bounds, with delay-dependent terms matching state-of-the-art first-order rates. For first-order feedback, we recover state-of-the-art regret bounds via a simpler, unified analysis.

Quantitatively, for bandit convex optimization we obtain O⁡(dtot+T34​k)O(\sqrt{d_{\text{tot}}}+T^{\frac{3}{4}}\sqrt{k}) regret, improving the delay-dependent term from O⁡(min⁡{T​dmax,(T​dtot)13})O(\min\{\sqrt{Td_{\text{max}}},(Td_{\text{tot}})^{\frac{1}{3}}\}) in previous work to O⁡(dtot)O(\sqrt{d_{\text{tot}}}). Here, kk, TT, dmaxd_{\text{max}}, and dtotd_{\text{tot}} denote the dimension, time horizon, maximum delay, and total delay, respectively. Under strong convexity, we achieve O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot}+(T2​ln⁡T)13​k23)O(\min\{\sigma_{\text{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\text{tot}}}\}+(T^{2}\ln T)^{\frac{1}{3}}{k}^{\frac{2}{3}}), improving the delay-dependent term from O⁡(dmax​ln⁡T)O(d_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T) in previous work to O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot})O(\min\{\sigma_{\text{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\text{tot}}}\}), where σmax\sigma_{\text{max}} denotes the maximum number of outstanding observations and may be considerably smaller than dmaxd_{\text{max}}.

1 Introduction

Online convex optimization (OCO) is a fundamental framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty Hazan and others (2016); Orabona (2019). In the classic OCO setting, a player repeatedly selects an action from a convex domain, incurs a loss specified by a convex loss function, and then receives feedback about that loss. In the full-information setting, the entire loss function is revealed. In the first-order setting, the player observes the gradient of the loss at the chosen action. In the zeroth-order (bandit) setting, the player observes only the scalar loss value.

In practice, observations are often delayed: feedback from round tt may arrive only at round t+dtt+d_{t}, where dtd_{t} is the round-dependent delay. This forces the player to make decisions without up-to-date information. For example, consider a recommendation system that must select content instantaneously for each arriving user. Feedback needed to update the system’s parameters (such as clicks or purchases) arrives only after user sessions conclude. When many users are served concurrently, new arrivals must be handled while feedback from earlier users is pending, resulting in delays. Delayed feedback has been studied extensively in many variants of sequential decision-making, including online learning, bandits, and reinforcement learning (e.g., Mesterharm, 2005; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2016; Zimmert and Seldin, 2020; van der Hoeven et al., 2023).

A natural question is whether delayed algorithms can be obtained as reductions from non-delayed ones. Prior work has made significant progress on this question (Weinberger and Ordentlich, 2002; Joulani et al., 2013; Joulani et al., 2016). However, existing approaches either require advance knowledge of the delay process, incur memory overhead scaling with the amount of outstanding feedback, or are limited to full-information feedback. Developing a unified, delay-adaptive reduction—one that requires no advance knowledge of delays, adapts to function regularity (e.g., strong convexity), and accommodates different feedback models (first-order or bandit)—is the main goal of this work.

In this paper, we introduce a continuous-time model for delayed feedback that subsumes the standard discrete-time model and enables a clean reduction from delayed feedback to immediate feedback for both online convex optimization with first-order feedback (OCO) and bandit convex optimization (BCO). For BCO, this reduction yields improved regret rates, while for OCO it recovers state-of-the-art bounds via a simple, unified analysis. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Continuous-time model (Section 3). We introduce a continuous-time model for delayed feedback. Instead of the usual round-based view in which each round reveals an unordered batch of observations, we place predictions and observations as events on a shared timeline, and show that the effective delay structure is induced by their interleaving. Theorem 3.4 characterizes this structure, identifying new invariants and equivalences among delay-related quantities that are widely used across the delayed-learning literature. Ordering the interaction by observation times provides a natural framework for analyzing algorithms that run single-instance updates upon each feedback arrival (e.g., Joulani et al. (2016)), yielding a regret decomposition into a non-delayed term and a prediction-drift term (Figure 4). Our analysis provides new tools for controlling this drift, which we exploit to improve regret bounds through a unified analysis, without requiring advance knowledge of problem parameters such as the maximum delay dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}}, total delay dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}}, maximum number of outstanding observations σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}, or the time horizon TT.

  2. 2.

    Reduction to non-delayed learning (Sections 4–5). Building on this decomposition, we reduce delayed OCO to online linear optimization with penalties for changing predictions, a problem with no delays. We provide wrappers that transform any algorithm for this setting into a delayed OCO or BCO algorithm whose regret is controlled by the base algorithm’s performance (Theorems 5.2 and 5.6). The BCO wrapper incorporates single-point gradient estimation (Flaxman et al., 2004).

  3. 3.

    First-order feedback (Section 5.1). Wrapping Proximal Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (P-FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) update rules recovers state-of-the-art bounds for delayed OCO: O⁡(dtot+T)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+\sqrt{T}) for convex losses (Corollary 5.3) and O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot}+ln⁡T)O(\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\}+\ln T) for strongly convex losses (Corollary 5.4), matching Quanrud and Khashabi (2015) and Qiu et al. (2025) respectively via an adaptive approach requiring no knowledge of delays or horizon.

  4. 4.

    Bandit feedback (Section 5.2). For delayed BCO, wrapping P-FTRL achieves O⁡(dtot+T3/4​k)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+T^{3/4}\sqrt{k}) expected regret (Corollary 5.7), where kk is the dimension of the domain, improving the delay dependence over (T​dtot)1/3(Td_{\textnormal{tot}})^{1/3} of Bistritz et al. (2022) and T​dmax\sqrt{Td_{\textnormal{max}}} of Wan et al. (2024). For strongly convex losses, we obtain O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot}+(T2​ln⁡T)1/3​k2/3)O(\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\}+(T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}{k}^{2/3}) regret (Corollary 5.8), improving over O⁡(dmax​ln⁡T+(T2​ln⁡T)1/3​k2/3)O(d_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T+(T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}{k}^{2/3}) of Wan et al. (2024). Note that σmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}} is always at most dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}}, and it can be much smaller in practice.11 1 For example, if d1=Θ⁡(T)d_{1}=\Theta(T) and dt=0d_{t}=0 for all t≥2t\geq 2, then dmax=dtot=Θ⁡(T)d_{\textnormal{max}}=d_{\textnormal{tot}}=\Theta(T) while σmax=1\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}=1. These results are summarized in Table 1.

  5. 5.

    Skipping scheme (Section 6). We incorporate the adaptive skipping technique of Zimmert and Seldin (2020), as an external wrapper (Algorithm 3), improving the delay term from O⁡(dtot)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}) to O⁡(minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+(∑t∉Qdt)12})O(\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\{|Q|+({\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t}})^{\frac{1}{2}}\}). This yields substantial gains when a few rounds have exceptionally large delays (Corollary 6.2).

  6. 6.

    Two-point bandit feedback (Appendix G). As a further application of our reduction, we give the first regret bounds for delayed BCO under the two-point feedback model of Agarwal et al. (2010). Using the standard two-point gradient estimator and its variance bound (Shamir, 2017), we obtain regret O⁡(dtot+T​k)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+\sqrt{Tk}) for convex losses and O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot}+k​ln⁡T)O(\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\}+k\ln T) under strong convexity.

Unified regret decomposition summary. Across all settings, our reduction approach yields regret bounds that decompose into a delay term dtot\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}, improvable via skipping to O⁡(minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+(∑t∉Qdt)12})O(\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\{|Q|+({\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t}})^{\frac{1}{2}}\}) (or min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot}\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\} for strongly convex losses), and a learning term matching the corresponding no-delay rate: T\sqrt{T} (or ln⁡T\ln T) for OCO with first-order feedback; T3/4​kT^{3/4}\sqrt{k} (or (T2​ln⁡T)1/3​k2/3(T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}k^{2/3}) for BCO; and T​k\sqrt{Tk} (or k​ln⁡Tk\ln T) for BCO with two-point feedback.

Related work. Methodologically, the work closest to ours is Joulani et al. (2016), who studied delayed OCO with full-information feedback. They propose a black-box-style reduction that feeds observations to a base (non-delayed) algorithm in order of arrival, bounding regret in terms of the base algorithm’s regret and prediction drift. With known dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}}, they achieve regret O⁡(T+dtot)O(\sqrt{T+d_{\textnormal{tot}}}). They also establish a bound of O⁡(T​τ∗)O(\sqrt{T\tau^{*}}), where τ∗\tau^{*} is the maximum number of observations that can arrive while some earlier feedback is still outstanding, known in advance. Using the tools developed in this paper, we show that τ∗=Θ⁡(dmax)\tau^{*}=\Theta(d_{\textnormal{max}}), thus expressing this result in standard notation as O⁡(T​dmax)O(\sqrt{Td_{\textnormal{max}}}).

Weinberger and Ordentlich (2002) first studied online learning with delayed feedback and proposed a reduction that runs dfixed+1d_{\text{fixed}}+1 parallel copies of a base non-delayed algorithm, yielding regret dfixed⋅R⁡(T/dfixed)d_{\text{fixed}}\cdot R(T/d_{\text{fixed}}) for a fixed, known delay dfixedd_{\text{fixed}}, where R⁡(T)R(T) denotes the base regret. Joulani et al. (2013) extended this to round-dependent delays, giving dmax⋅R⁡(T/dmax)d_{\textnormal{max}}\cdot R(T/d_{\textnormal{max}}). Quanrud and Khashabi (2015) showed that, in delayed OCO, a simple delayed gradient-descent scheme, updating each round using whatever gradients have arrived so far with stepsize η≍1/T+dtot\eta\asymp 1/\sqrt{T+d_{\textnormal{tot}}}, achieves regret O⁡(dtot+T)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+\sqrt{T}). Delayed OCO with strongly convex losses has also received attention (Wan et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025).

Héliou et al. (2020) first extended the bandit gradient descent method of Flaxman et al. (2004) to delayed BCO. Bistritz et al. (2022) developed the first fully delay-adaptive algorithm using a doubling trick with respect to both horizon and total delay, and Wan et al. (2024) improved the bound via a blocking strategy; however, their method requires advance knowledge of dmaxd_{\textnormal{max}} and TT.

For additional related work on online convex optimization and online learning with delayed feedback, see Appendix A.

2 Problem Setting

Let T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} denote the time horizon, and let 𝒦⊂ℝk\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} be a non-empty, convex, and closed domain for the dimension k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. We equip ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} with a norm ∥.∥\|.\| and its dual norm ∥.∥⋆\|.\|_{\star}.

The player interacts with an environment determined by an oblivious adversary over TT rounds (Figure 1). Before the game begins, the adversary selects delays dtd_{t} and convex, differentiable loss functions ft:𝒦→ℝf_{t}:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} for each round. Every round tt, the player predicts xt∈𝒦x_{t}\in\mathcal{K}, receiving the corresponding feedback (gradient ∇ft​(xt)\nabla f_{t}(x_{t}) or value ft​(xt)f_{t}(x_{t}), depending on the feedback model) at the end of round t+dtt+d_{t}. We assume dt∈[T−t]d_{t}\in[T-t] for all t∈[T]t\in[T], since feedback arriving after round TT cannot affect any prediction.

The regret against a comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K} is defined as RT​(u)=∑t=1T(ft​(xt)−ft​(u))R_{T}(u)=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(f_{t}(x_{t})-f_{t}(u)), and its expected regret as R¯T​(u)=𝔼⁡[RT​(u)]\widebar{R}_{T}(u)=\mathbb{E}[R_{T}(u)]. Letting x∗∈argminx∈𝒦∑t=1Tft(x)x^{*}\in\argmin_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(x) denote the best action in hindsight, the objective is to minimize RT​(x∗)R_{T}(x^{*}) almost surely or its expectation R¯T​(x∗)\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*}).

Regularity assumptions.

We impose the following standard regularity assumptions, which are necessary to obtain sublinear regret guarantees in online convex optimization.

Assumption 2.1.

The diameter of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is bounded by DD, i.e., supx,y∈𝒦‖x−y‖≤D\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{K}}\left\|x-y\right\|\leq D.

Assumption 2.2.

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], ftf_{t} has norm of its gradient bounded by G≥0G\geq 0, i.e., supx∈𝒦‖∇ft​(x)‖⋆≤G\sup_{x\in\mathcal{K}}\left\|\nabla f_{t}(x)\right\|_{\star}\leq G.

Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold throughout the paper. When deriving stronger guarantees, we also impose the following strong convexity condition, stated explicitly when invoked.

Assumption 2.3.

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], ftf_{t} is λ\lambda-strongly convex for λ>0\lambda>0, i.e., ft​(y)≥ft​(x)+⟨∇ft​(x),y−x⟩+λ2​‖y−x‖2f_{t}(y)\geq f_{t}(x)+\langle{\nabla f_{t}(x),\,y-x}\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\left\|y-x\right\|^{2} for all x,y∈𝒦x,y\in\mathcal{K}.

For bandit convex optimization, we take ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| to be the Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} and impose two additional assumptions.

Assumption 2.4.

For all t∈[T]t\in[T], absolute values of ftf_{t} are bounded by M≥0M\geq 0, i.e., supx∈𝒦|ft​(x)|≤M\sup_{x\in\mathcal{K}}|f_{t}(x)|\leq M.

Assumption 2.5.

The domain satisfies r​𝔹k⊆𝒦⊆R​𝔹kr\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K}\subseteq R\mathbb{B}^{k} for some radii 0<r<R0<r<R.

Remark 2.6 (Differentiability of loss functions).

While we assume throughout that the loss functions ftf_{t} are differentiable, weaker regularity suffices: for first-order feedback, subdifferentiability with subgradient norms bounded by GG, and for bandit feedback, integrability with GG-Lipschitzness. We do not pursue this generality as it does not materially affect the analysis or the resulting bounds.

Steady algorithms. An algorithm in this setting is a (possibly randomized) mapping from the history of received feedback and information about delays to predictions. The class of steady algorithms is formally defined below.

Definition 2.7 (Steady Algorithm).

An algorithm for online learning with delays is steady if it does not change its prediction after rounds without feedback: xt=xt+1x_{t}=x_{t+1} whenever {s:s+ds=t}=∅\{s:s+d_{s}=t\}=\emptyset. It is steady in expectation if 𝔼⁡[xt]=𝔼⁡[xt+1]\mathbb{E}[x_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[x_{t+1}] whenever {s:s+ds=t}=∅\{s:s+d_{s}=t\}=\emptyset.

Notation. For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we let [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. For any sequence {at}t=1T\{\mathrm{a}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, indexed over [T][T], we write atot=∑t=1Tat\mathrm{a}_{\textnormal{tot}}=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{a}_{t} and amax=maxt∈[T]⁡at\mathrm{a}_{\textnormal{max}}=\max_{t\in[T]}\mathrm{a}_{t}. We denote by 𝔹k\mathbb{B}^{k} and 𝕊k−1\mathbb{S}^{k-1} the unit Euclidean ball and sphere centered at the origin in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}, respectively. For any S⊆ℝkS\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k} and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, we let c​S={c​x:x∈S}cS=\{cx:x\in S\}.

3 Continuous Time Model for Delays

The classical formulation of online learning with delays assumes a discrete, round-based time structure: a player makes a prediction in round tt and receives feedback in round t+dtt+d_{t}. Real-world systems, however, generate predictions and observations asynchronously. Rather than forcing these events into discrete rounds, we adopt a continuous time model that places them on a timeline ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}.

Definition 3.1 (Continuous Time Model (CTM)).

The timing of predictions and observations is determined by latency-intervals {It}t=1T\{I_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, where It=(lt,rt)⊂ℝ+I_{t}=(l_{t},r_{t})\subset\mathbb{R}_{+}. For every t∈[T]t\in[T], the environment requests a prediction at time ltl_{t} and reveals the corresponding observation at time rtr_{t}. All timestamps {lt,rt}t=1T\{l_{t},r_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} are distinct, and intervals are indexed in increasing order of prediction times: 0<l1<…<lT0<l_{1}<\ldots<l_{T}.

In the round-based model, the delay sequence {dt}t=1T\{d_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} fully specifies the time structure. In particular, it determines the number of outstanding observations in each round, σt=∑s=1t−1𝕀(s+ds≥t)\sigma_{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\ind(s+d_{s}\geq t), which is commonly used in the literature; for brevity, we refer to σt\sigma_{t} as the backlog in this paper. Under the CTM, both delays and backlogs arise directly from the geometry of the latency intervals.

Section 3.1 formalizes this structure. Building on it, Section 3.2 introduces an observation-centric view of the problem that complements the standard prediction-centric perspective. We show that steady algorithms admit a natural regret decomposition: non-delayed regret on observation-ordered losses plus delay-induced prediction drift (Fig. 4).

3.1 Delays, Backlogs, and Their Duals

Under the CTM, rounds of the delayed problem (Fig. 1) naturally correspond to time-intervals: round tt spans the interval [lt,lt+1)[l_{t},l_{t+1}), during which the tt-th prediction is made at time ltl_{t}, and observations arrive at times {rs:rs∈(lt,lt+1)}\{r_{s}:r_{s}\in(l_{t},l_{t+1})\}. Therefore, the discrete delay dtd_{t} and backlog σt\sigma_{t} arise as

dt=|{s:ls∈It}|andσt=|{s:lt∈Is}|,\displaystyle d_{t}=|\{s:\,l_{s}\in I_{t}\}|\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma_{t}=|\{s:\,l_{t}\in I_{s}\}|, (1)

where dtd_{t} counts how many predictions are made between the tt-th prediction and observing its feedback, and σt\sigma_{t} counts how many previous predictions still await feedback immediately before making the tt-th prediction.

The following lemma and remark show that these definitions recover the classical round-based formulation.

Lemma 3.2.

For quantities in (1), it holds that:

rt∈(lt+dt,lt+dt+1),σt=|{s:s<t≤s+ds}|.\displaystyle r_{t}\in(l_{t+d_{t}},l_{t+d_{t}+1}),\quad\sigma_{t}=|\{s:s<t\leq s+d_{s}\}|.
Proof.

Exactly |{s:ls<rt}|=|{s:ls≤lt}|+|{s:lt<ls<rt}|=t+dt|\{s\!:\!l_{s}\!<\!r_{t}\}|=|\{s\!:l_{s}\!\leq\!l_{t}\}|\!+\!|\{s\!:\!l_{t}\!<\!l_{s}\!<\!r_{t}\}|=t+d_{t} prediction times precede time rtr_{t}, so rt∈(lt+dt,lt+dt+1)r_{t}\in(l_{t+d_{t}},l_{t+d_{t}+1}). Then, the identity for backlog σt=|{s:ls<lt<rs}|\sigma_{t}=|\{s:l_{s}<l_{t}<r_{s}\}| follows immediately. ∎

Remark 3.3 (Consistency and Realizability in the CTM).

Lemma 3.2 confirms that our definitions are consistent with round-based protocols: dtd_{t} equals the number of round-intervals [ls,ls+1)[l_{s},l_{s+1}) spanned by ItI_{t}, placing observation time rtr_{t} in round t+dtt+d_{t}; σt\sigma_{t} matches the classical definition as the number of outstanding delays. Conversely, any round-based delayed-feedback protocol can be represented within the CTM. Specifically, given a delay sequence {dt}t=1T\{d_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, we can set (lt,rt)=(t,t+dt+1−2−t)(l_{t},r_{t})=(t,t+d_{t}+1-2^{-t}) so that round tt spans interval [t,t+1)[t,t+1) and observation time rtr_{t} clearly falls within round t+dtt+d_{t} spanned by interval [t+dt,t+dt+1)[t+d_{t},t+d_{t}+1).

To fully characterize the delay structure in the CTM, we define novel dual-delay and dual-backlog sequences

dt⋆=|{s:rs∈It}|andσt⋆=|{s:rt∈Is}|.\displaystyle d^{\star}_{t}=|\{s:\,r_{s}\in I_{t}\}|\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma^{\star}_{t}=|\{s:\,r_{t}\in I_{s}\}|. (2)

Here, dual-delay dt⋆d^{\star}_{t} counts how many observations occur between the tt-th prediction and its observation, while σt⋆\sigma^{\star}_{t} counts how many predictions still await feedback when receiving observation for the tt-th prediction.

The following theorem establishes the fundamental properties and relations among the four sequences.

Theorem 3.4.

For quantities in (1) and (2), it holds that:

  1. (a)

    ∑t=1Tdt=∑t=1Tσt=∑t=1Tdt⋆=∑t=1Tσt⋆\sum_{t=1}^{T}d_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}d^{\star}_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma^{\star}_{t},

  2. (b)

    σmax=σmax⋆,12​dmax≤dmax⋆≤2​dmax\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}=\sigma^{\star}_{\textnormal{max}},\quad\tfrac{1}{2}d_{\textnormal{max}}\leq d^{\star}_{\textnormal{max}}\leq 2d_{\textnormal{max}},

  3. (c)

    dt⋆=σt+β⁡(t)−t,σt⋆=dt+t−β⁡(t)d^{\star}_{t}=\sigma_{t}+\beta(t)-t,\quad\sigma^{\star}_{t}=d_{t}+t-\beta(t),

where β:[T]→[T]\beta\!:\![T]\!\to\![T] is the permutation β⁡(t)=|{s:rs≤rt}|\beta(t)\!=\!|\{s\!:\!r_{s}\!\leq\!r_{t}\}|.

In particular, all four sequences sum to the total delay dtotd_{\textnormal{tot}}. Figure 2 illustrates this in a concrete example: delays dtd_{t} (dual-delays dt⋆d^{\star}_{t}) correspond to black (white) triangles along intervals ItI_{t}, while backlogs σt\sigma_{t} (dual-backlogs σt⋆\sigma^{\star}_{t}) correspond to black (white) triangles at timestamps ltl_{t} (rtr_{t}), with the total number of triangles of each color dtot=6d_{\textnormal{tot}}=6.

See Appendix C for proofs of the results in this section, as well as additional properties of the CTM.

3.2 Observation-Ordering and Steady Algorithms

The CTM naturally suggests an observation-centric perspective, in which we order quantities by observation times rather than by prediction times. This viewpoint complements the standard prediction-centric view in the literature and is essential for our analysis of steady algorithms. To facilitate this, we introduce the notational convention for observation-ordering, which we adopt throughout the paper.

Definition 3.5 (Observation-Ordering).

Under the CTM, let ρ:[T]→[T]\rho\!:\![T]\!\to\![T] be the permutation such that rρ⁡(1)<…<rρ⁡(T)r_{\rho(1)}\!<\!...\!<\!r_{\rho(T)}. For any sequence {at}t=1T\{\mathrm{a}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} indexed by t∈[T]t\in[T], define its observation-ordering {a~n}n=1T\{\widetilde{\mathrm{a}}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T} by a~n=aρ⁡(n)\widetilde{\mathrm{a}}_{n}=\mathrm{a}_{\rho(n)} for n∈[T]n\in[T].

For ease of notation, we use subscripts n∈[T]n\in[T] for observation-ordered quantities and t∈[T]t\in[T] for prediction-ordered quantities throughout the paper.

Under observation-ordering, the nn-th observation arrives at time r~n\widetilde{r}_{n} for the prediction x~n\widetilde{x}_{n} made at time l~n\widetilde{l}_{n} and evaluated on loss function f~n\widetilde{f}_{n}. Setting r~0=0\widetilde{r}_{0}\!=\!0, we obtain a chronological sequence of observation times 0=r~0<r~1<…<r~T0=\widetilde{r}_{0}<\widetilde{r}_{1}<\ldots<\widetilde{r}_{T} such that all timestamps lie within [r~0,r~T][\widetilde{r}_{0},\widetilde{r}_{T}]. Since no two timestamps coincide, each prediction time l~n\widetilde{l}_{n} lies strictly between two consecutive observation times {r~n}n=0T\{\widetilde{r}_{n}\}_{n=0}^{T}. The following lemma, the observation-centric analogue of Lemma 3.2, characterizes this interleaving and expresses the dual-backlog σ~n⋆\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n} as the number of outstanding dual-delays.

Lemma 3.6.

For quantities in (2), it holds that:

l~n∈(r~n−d~n⋆−1,r~n−d~n⋆),σ~n⋆=|{m:m−d~m⋆≤n<m}|.\displaystyle\widetilde{l}_{n}\!\in\!(\widetilde{r}_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}-1},\widetilde{r}_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}}),\quad\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}\!=\!|\{m\!:\!m\!-\!\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}\!\leq\!n\!<\!m\}|.
Proof.

Exactly |{m:r~m<l~n}|=|{m:r~m<r~n}|−|{m:l~n<r~m<r~n}|=n−−d~n⋆|\{m\!:\!\widetilde{r}_{m}\!<\!\widetilde{l}_{n}\}|\!=\!|\{m\!:\widetilde{r}_{m}\!<\!\widetilde{r}_{n}\}|\!-\!|\{m\!:\!\widetilde{l}_{n}\!<\!\widetilde{r}_{m}\!<\widetilde{r}_{n}\}|=n\!-\!1\!-\!\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n} observations precede time l~n\widetilde{l}_{n}, so l~n∈(r~n−d~n⋆−1,r~n−d~n⋆)\widetilde{l}_{n}\in(\widetilde{r}_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}-1},\widetilde{r}_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}}). The identity for dual-backlog σ~n⋆=|{m:l~m<r~n<r~m}|\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}=|\{m:\widetilde{l}_{m}<\widetilde{r}_{n}<\widetilde{r}_{m}\}| follows immediately. ∎

The observation-centric perspective is particularly useful for analyzing steady algorithms (Definition 2.7). Since a steady algorithm does not change its prediction in rounds without feedback, it admits a base-prediction sequence {zn}n=1T⊂𝒦\{z_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T}\subset\mathcal{K} such that the prediction remains constant between consecutive observation times: for each n∈[T]n\in[T] and every prediction time lt∈(r~n−1,r~n)l_{t}\in(\widetilde{r}_{n-1},\widetilde{r}_{n}), the algorithm outputs xt=znx_{t}=z_{n}. Equivalently, the rounds [T][T] partition into sets Zn={t:lt∈[r~n−1,r~n)}Z_{n}=\{t:l_{t}\in[\widetilde{r}_{n-1},\widetilde{r}_{n})\}, with xt=znx_{t}=z_{n} if and only if t∈Znt\in Z_{n}. Figure 3 illustrates this for the example in Figure 2.

Lemma 3.6 links the observation-ordered predictions to the base-predictions through the dual-delays: x~n=zn−d~n⋆\widetilde{x}_{n}=z_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}}. Substituting this identity, we can write the regret of any steady algorithm entirely in terms of the base sequence zn{z_{n}} evaluated on the observation-ordered losses f~n{\widetilde{f}_{n}}. For GG-Lipschitz losses, this yields the following decomposition:

Here, the non-delayed regret is the regret of the sequence {zn}n=1T\{z_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T} on the observation-ordered losses {f~n}n=1T\{\widetilde{f}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T} and the prediction drift captures the cost of the played predictions x~n=zn−d~n⋆\widetilde{x}_{n}=z_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}} lagging behind base-predictions znz_{n}.

This decomposition underlies our reduction from online learning with delays to online learning with drift-penalization, which we define in the following section.

4 Online Learning with Drift Penalization

This section introduces online linear optimization with drift penalization (Figure 5), a game that serves as the foundation for reductions in subsequent sections. Crucially, this formulation involves no delays; the connection to delayed feedback emerges only through the reductions.

In this game, a player selects predictions from 𝒦\mathcal{K} (the same domain as in OCO with delays) over NN rounds, incurring in each round a linear loss and a penalty for moving too far from past predictions, measured against one of them. Specifically, in round nn, the player chooses znz_{n} and incurs the loss ⟨cn,zn⟩\langle{c_{n},z_{n}}\rangle plus the drift penalty ‖zn−zn−λn‖\|z_{n}-z_{n-\lambda_{n}}\|, specified by the lag λn\lambda_{n}. The loss vectors and lags {cn,λn}n=1N\{c_{n},\lambda_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} are fixed by an adversary before the game begins. To update his strategy, after each round the player observes (cn,λn)(c_{n},\lambda_{n}) as well as the number of outstanding lags νn=|{m:m−λm≤n<m}|\nu_{n}=|\{m:m-\lambda_{m}\!\leq n<m\}|, which summarizes how many future penalties will involve predictions up to the current round nn.

To measure performance, we define the drift-penalized regret with weight W≥0W\geq 0 against a comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K} as

ℜNdrift​(u,W)=ℜN​(u)+W​𝔇N,\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{N}(u;W)=\mathfrak{R}_{N}(u)+W\mathfrak{D}_{N}, (3)

where ℜN​(u)=∑n=1N⟨cn,zn−u⟩\mathfrak{R}_{N}(u)=\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\langle{c_{n},z_{n}-u}\rangle is the standard regret and 𝔇N=∑n=1N‖zn−λn−zn‖\mathfrak{D}_{N}=\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\|z_{n-\lambda_{n}}\!-\!z_{n}\| is the total drift penalty.

Any online linear optimization algorithm applies to this setting, with its standard regret bounding ℜN​(u)\mathfrak{R}_{N}(u); moreover, stable algorithms naturally incur smaller drift penalty 𝔇N\mathfrak{D}_{N}.

P-FTRL and OMD Updates.

We analyze how Proximal Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (P-FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) perform in online learning with drift penalization. Given a non-increasing learning rate sequence {ηn}n=1N⊂(0,∞)\{\eta_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}\subset(0,\infty) and initial point z1∈𝒦z_{1}\in\mathcal{K}, these algorithms select predictions sequentially according to the following respective update rules:

P-FTRL:zn+1\displaystyle\textnormal{P-FTRL}\colon z_{n+1}\! =argminz∈𝒦∑m=1n(⟨cm,z⟩+αn​‖zm−z‖22),\displaystyle=\!\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{K}}\!\sum_{m\!=\!1}^{n}\!\left(\langle{c_{m},z}\rangle+\tfrac{\alpha_{n}\left\|z_{m}\!-\!z\right\|^{2}}{2}\right)\!, (4)
OMD:zn+1\displaystyle\textnormal{OMD}\colon z_{n+1}\! =argminz∈𝒦(⟨cn,z⟩+‖zn−z‖22​ηn),\displaystyle=\!\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{K}}\left(\langle{c_{n},z}\rangle+\tfrac{\left\|z_{n}\!-\!z\right\|^{2}}{2\eta_{n}}\right), (5)

where {αn}n=1N\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} is given by α1=1η1,αn+1=1ηn+1−1ηn\alpha_{1}=\tfrac{1}{\eta_{1}},\alpha_{n+1}=\tfrac{1}{\eta_{n+1}}-\tfrac{1}{\eta_{n}}. The following theorem provides regret and drift guarantees.

Theorem 4.1.

For every u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}, predictions {zn}n=1T\{z_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T} generated by P-FTRL (4) or OMD (5) satisfy

ℜN​(u)\displaystyle\mathfrak{R}_{N}(u) ≤∑n=1N1ηn−1ηn−12​‖zn−u‖2+12​∑n=1Nηn​‖cn‖⋆2,\displaystyle\leq\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\tfrac{\frac{1}{\eta_{n}}-\frac{1}{\eta_{n-1}}}{2}\left\|z_{n}\!-\!u\right\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\eta_{n}\|c_{n}\|_{\star}^{2},
𝔇N\displaystyle\mathfrak{D}_{N} ≤∑n=1Nηn​νn​‖cn‖⋆.\displaystyle\leq\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\eta_{n}\nu_{n}\|c_{n}\|_{\star}.

The regret bound is standard (e.g., Orabona (2019)). The drift bound arises by decomposing drift into single-step terms satisfying ‖zn+1−zn‖≤ηn​‖cn‖⋆\|z_{n+1}-z_{n}\|\leq\eta_{n}\|c_{n}\|_{\star}; the resulting dependence on νn\nu_{n} is the key to our delay-adaptive analysis. We also establish a novel drift guarantee for P-FTRL, which is essential for our delayed BCO results.

Lemma 4.2.

P-FTRL (4) generates {zn}n=1T\{z_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T} such that

𝔇N≤∑n=1Nηn​‖∑m=n−λnn−1cm‖⋆+D​Hη,\displaystyle\mathfrak{D}_{N}\leq\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\eta_{n}\|\textstyle\sum_{m=n-\lambda_{n}}^{n-1}c_{m}\|_{\star}+D\,H_{\eta},

where Hη=∑n=1N(1−ηnηn−λn)H_{\eta}=\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}(1-\frac{\eta_{n}}{\eta_{n-\lambda_{n}}}) and DD is an upper bound on the diameter of 𝒦\mathcal{K} (Assumption 2.1).

5 Blackbox Reductions and Main Results

Here, we develop algorithms for delayed OCO and BCO via reduction to drift-penalized online linear optimization. The key construction is a wrapper 𝒲OCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}} (Algorithm 1) that takes any algorithm ℬ\mathcal{B} for drift-penalized OLO as a blackbox and produces a new algorithm 𝒲OCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B}) for delayed OCO. The wrapper feeds observation-ordered gradients g~n=∇f~n​(x~n)\widetilde{g}_{n}=\nabla\widetilde{f}_{n}(\widetilde{x}_{n}) as loss vectors to ℬ\mathcal{B}, with dual-delays d~n⋆\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n} as lags and dual-backlogs σ~n⋆\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n} as numbers of outstanding lags. The base algorithm ℬ\mathcal{B} produces base-predictions that the wrapper outputs as its own predictions. An analogous wrapper 𝒲BCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}} (Algorithm 2) handles bandit feedback by using single-point gradient estimates from the classical work by Flaxman et al. (2004).

Remark 5.1 (Feasibility).

This reduction is feasible because (i) the dual-backlog σ~n⋆\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n} equals the number of outstanding dual-delays by Lemma 3.6, and (ii) the wrapper runs updates on ℬ\mathcal{B} only at observation times r~n\widetilde{r}_{n}, when all required quantities are available. Specifically, at time r~n\widetilde{r}_{n}, the gradient g~n=∇f~n​(x~n)\widetilde{g}_{n}=\nabla\widetilde{f}_{n}(\widetilde{x}_{n}) (or the value f~n​(x~n)\widetilde{f}_{n}(\widetilde{x}_{n}) in the case of bandit feedback) is revealed, while the dual-delay d~n⋆=|{m:l~n<r~m<r~n}|\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}=|\{m:\widetilde{l}_{n}<\widetilde{r}_{m}<\widetilde{r}_{n}\}| and the dual-backlog σ~n⋆=|{m:l~m<r~n<r~m}|\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}=|\{m:\widetilde{l}_{m}<\widetilde{r}_{n}<\widetilde{r}_{m}\}| can be computed from the observed history up to time r~n\widetilde{r}_{n}.

5.1 Delayed OCO via Drift-Penalized OLO

We now present the wrapper 𝒲OCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}} for delayed online convex optimization with first-order feedback. The wrapper maintains a current base-prediction z¯\widebar{z} initialized by ℬ\mathcal{B}, outputs z¯\widebar{z} whenever a prediction is requested, and updates z¯\widebar{z} by forwarding each received gradient to ℬ\mathcal{B} along with the dual-delay and dual-backlog.

By construction, this algorithm is steady: it updates only upon receiving feedback and outputs the current base-prediction otherwise. Effectively, the algorithm updates ℬ\mathcal{B} sequentially on observation-ordered tuples (g~n,d~n⋆,σ~n⋆)(\widetilde{g}_{n},\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n},\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}), where g~n=∇f~n​(x~n)\widetilde{g}_{n}=\nabla\widetilde{f}_{n}(\widetilde{x}_{n}) (i.e., gt=∇ft​(xt)g_{t}=\nabla f_{t}(x_{t})), producing base-predictions znz_{n} at observation times r~n−1\widetilde{r}_{n-1} that yield predictions x~m=zm−d~m⋆\widetilde{x}_{m}=z_{m-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}} at prediction times l~m∈(r~m−d~m⋆−1,r~m−d~m⋆)\widetilde{l}_{m}\in(\widetilde{r}_{m-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}-1},\widetilde{r}_{m-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}}).

The following theorem shows that the regret of 𝒲OCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B}) is controlled through the drift-penalized regret of ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Theorem 5.2 (Regret of Algorithm 1).

For any base algorithm ℬ\mathcal{B} and comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}, 𝒲OCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B}) guarantees

RT​(u)≤ℜTdrift​(u,G),\displaystyle R_{T}(u)\leq\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;G),

where ℜTdrift​(u,W)\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;W) is the drift-penalized regret (3) of ℬ\mathcal{B} for loss vectors cn=g~nc_{n}=\widetilde{g}_{n} and lags λn=d~n⋆\lambda_{n}=\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}.

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), it further holds that

RT​(u)≤ℜTdrift​(u,3​G)−λ2​∑n=1T‖zn−u‖2.\displaystyle R_{T}(u)\leq\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;3G)-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{T}\|z_{n}\!-\!u\|^{2}.

Instantiating ℬ\mathcal{B} with P-FTRL (4) or OMD (5) with appropriate learning rates yields the following guarantees.

Corollary 5.3.

𝒲OCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B}), where ℬ\mathcal{B} runs P-FTRL (4) or OMD (5) with ηn=D/Gn+∑m=1nσ~m⋆\eta_{n}=\frac{D/G}{\sqrt{n+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{m}}}, guarantees

RT​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​[dtot+T]).\displaystyle R_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(GD\,\left[\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+\sqrt{T}\right]\right).
Corollary 5.4.

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), 𝒲OCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B}), where ℬ\mathcal{B} runs P-FTRL (4) with ηn=1n​λ\eta_{n}=\tfrac{1}{n\lambda}, guarantees

RT(x∗)=O(G2λ[min{(σmaxlnT,dtot}+lnT]).\displaystyle R_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}\left[\min\left\{(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\right\}+\ln T\right]\right).

Running OMD (5) with ηn=1n​λ\eta_{n}=\frac{1}{n\lambda} instead guarantees

RT​(x∗)=O⁡(G2λ​(σmax+1)​ln⁡T).\displaystyle R_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\!+\!1)\ln T\right).

In both corollaries, the learning rates form a deterministic sequence that can be computed online: ηn\eta_{n} depends only on nn and the dual-backlogs σ~1⋆,…,σ~n⋆\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}, all of which are available at the nn-th update. The proofs apply Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 with our chosen learning rates. Details are deferred to Appendix E.

5.2 Delayed BCO via Drift-Penalized OLO

We adapt the wrapper approach to bandit convex optimization, where only scalar loss values are observed, by using single-point gradient estimation from Flaxman et al. (2004).

Under Assumption 2.5, i.e., r​𝔹k⊆𝒦⊆R​𝔹kr\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K}\subseteq R\mathbb{B}^{k}, we have (1−δ/r)​𝒦+δ​𝔹k⊆𝒦(1-\delta/r)\,\mathcal{K}+\delta\,\mathbb{B}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{K} for all δ∈(0,r]\delta\in(0,r]. This allows us to define, for any δ∈(0,r]\delta\in(0,r] and integrable f:𝒦→ℝf:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R}, the δ\delta-smoothing of ff as fδ:(1−δ/r)​𝒦→ℝf^{\delta}:(1-\delta/r)\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{R} given by fδ​(x)=𝔼v∼Unif​(𝔹k)​[f⁡(x+δ​v)]f^{\delta}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{B}^{k})}[f(x+\delta v)]. The key properties of this construction are summarized in the following theorem.

Theorem 5.5 (Single-Point Gradient Estimation, Flaxman et al. (2004)).

For any δ∈(0,r]\delta\!\in\!(0,\!r] and integrable f:𝒦→ℝf:\mathcal{K}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}:

  1. 1.

    The δ\delta-smoothing fδf^{\delta} is differentiable with gradients ∇fδ​(x)=kδ​𝔼u∼Unif​(𝕊k−1)​[f⁡(x+δ​u)​u]\nabla f^{\delta}(x)=\tfrac{k}{\delta}\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1})}[f(x+\delta u)\,u].

  2. 2.

    If ff is convex (λ\lambda-strongly convex), so is fδf^{\delta}.

  3. 3.

    If ff is GG-Lipschitz, then |fδ​(x)−f⁡(x)|≤G​δ|f^{\delta}(x)-f(x)|\leq G\delta and ‖∇fδ​(x)‖≤G\|\nabla f^{\delta}(x)\|\leq G for x∈(1−δ/r)​𝒦x\in(1-\delta/r)\mathcal{K}.

The wrapper 𝒲BCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}} (Algorithm 2) follows the structure of 𝒲OCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}, but replaces true gradients with single-point estimates. The algorithm takes as input a non-increasing sequence of smoothing parameters (δt)t≥1⊂(0,r](\delta_{t})_{t\geq 1}\subset(0,r], that can be specified independently of horizon TT when it’s unknown. In round tt, given the current base-prediction yt=z¯y_{t}=\widebar{z} from ℬ\mathcal{B}, the algorithm samples an exploration direction ut∼Unif​(𝕊k−1)u_{t}\!\sim\!\textnormal{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}), predicts xt=(1−δt/r)​yt+δt​utx_{t}=(1-\delta_{t}/r)y_{t}+\delta_{t}u_{t}, and upon receiving loss fs​(xs)f_{s}(x_{s}) constructs the gradient estimate g^sδ=kδs​fs​(xs)​us\widehat{g}^{\delta}_{s}=\tfrac{k}{\delta_{s}}f_{s}(x_{s})u_{s}, which it forwards to ℬ\mathcal{B} along with dual-delay ds⋆d^{\star}_{s} and dual-backlog σs⋆\sigma^{\star}_{s} to update z¯\widebar{z}. By Theorem 5.5, we have 𝔼⁡[g^tδ∣yt]=∇ftδt​((1−δt/r)​yt)\mathbb{E}[\widehat{g}^{\delta}_{t}\mid y_{t}]=\nabla f^{\delta_{t}}_{t}((1-\delta_{t}/r)y_{t}) for all t∈[T]t\in[T].

Unlike the OCO case, the resulting algorithm is not steady due to random exploration, but is steady in expectation for a fixed schedule δt=δ\delta_{t}=\delta. Nevertheless, since the current base-prediction is updated only upon receiving feedback, the same analysis applies. The algorithm updates ℬ\mathcal{B} sequentially on tuples (g^~nδ,d~n⋆,σ~n⋆)(\widetilde{\widehat{g}}^{\delta}_{n},\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n},\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}), where g^~nδ=kδ~n​f~n​(x~n)​u~n\widetilde{\widehat{g}}^{\delta}_{n}=\tfrac{k}{\widetilde{\delta}_{n}}\widetilde{f}_{n}(\widetilde{x}_{n})\widetilde{u}_{n}, producing base-predictions znz_{n} that yield predictions x~n=(1−δ~n/r)​y~n+δ~n​u~n\widetilde{x}_{n}=(1-\widetilde{\delta}_{n}/r)\widetilde{y}_{n}+\widetilde{\delta}_{n}\widetilde{u}_{n} with y~n=zn−d~n⋆\widetilde{y}_{n}=z_{n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}}.

The following theorem bounds the expected regret of 𝒲BCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}}(\mathcal{B}) in terms of the drift-penalized regret of ℬ\mathcal{B}, with an additional bias of order δtot=∑t=1Tδt\delta_{\textnormal{tot}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_{t} due to smoothing.

Theorem 5.6 (Regret of Algorithm 2).

For any base-algorithm ℬ\mathcal{B}, non-increasing sequence (δt)t≥1⊂(0,r](\delta_{t})_{t\geq 1}\subset(0,r], and comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K}, 𝒲BCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}}(\mathcal{B}) guarantees

R¯T​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(u) ≤𝔼⁡[ℜTdrift​(u,G)]+6​G​R​δtotr,\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;G)\right]+\tfrac{6GR\delta_{\textnormal{tot}}}{r},

where ℜTdrift​(u,W)\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;W) is the drift-penalized regret (3) of ℬ\mathcal{B} for loss vectors cn=g^~nδc_{n}=\widetilde{\widehat{g}}^{\delta}_{n} and lags λn=d~n⋆\lambda_{n}=\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}.

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), it further holds that

R¯T​(u)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(u) ≤𝔼⁡[ℜTdrift​(u,3​G)−λ2​∑n=1T‖zn−u‖2]+10​G​R​δtotr.\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathfrak{R}^{\textnormal{drift}}_{T}(u;3G)\!-\!\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\!\textstyle\sum_{n=1}^{T}\|z_{n}\!-\!u\|^{2}\right]\!+\!\tfrac{10GR\delta_{\textnormal{tot}}}{r}.

Selecting an appropriate smoothing sequence (δt)t≥1(\delta_{t})_{t\geq 1} and instantiating ℬ\mathcal{B} with P-FTRL (4) yields concrete guarantees. To state them, we introduce the smoothness ratio ν=MG​r\nu=\frac{M}{Gr}, measuring gradient magnitude relative to the curvature-adjusted domain size, where MM is the absolute value bound (Assumption 2.4). Since the nn-th update occurs in round ρ⁡(n)+dρ⁡(n)\rho(n)+d_{\rho(n)}, the observation round of feedback from round ρ⁡(n)\rho(n), the smoothing parameter δn′=δρ⁡(n)+dρ⁡(n)\delta^{\prime}_{n}=\delta_{\rho(n)+d_{\rho(n)}} is available and can be incorporated into the learning rate ηn\eta_{n}.

Corollary 5.7.

𝒲BCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}}(\mathcal{B}), where (δt)t≥1(\delta_{t})_{t\geq 1} is set to either a round-dependent schedule δt=r​min⁡{1,ν​kt1/4}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\nu k}}{t^{1/4}}\right\} or a fixed schedule δt=r​min⁡{1,ν​kT1/4}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\nu k}}{T^{1/4}}\right\} and ℬ\mathcal{B} runs P-FTRL (4) with ηn=D/Gn+∑m=1n(σ~m⋆+(ν​k​r/δm′)2)\eta_{n}=\frac{D/G}{\sqrt{n+\sum_{m=1}^{n}(\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{m}+({\nu kr}/{\delta^{\prime}_{m}})^{2})}}, guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​[dtot+T3/4​ν​k]).\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\left(GD\left[\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}+T^{3/4}\sqrt{\nu k}\right]\right).
Corollary 5.8.

Under λ\lambda-strong convexity (2.3), 𝒲BCO​(ℬ)\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}}(\mathcal{B}), where (δt)t≥1(\delta_{t})_{t\geq 1} is set to either a round-dependent schedule δt=r​min⁡{1,(ν2​k2​ln⁡tt)1/3}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,(\tfrac{\nu^{2}{k}^{2}\ln t}{t})^{1/3}\right\} or a fixed schedule δt=r​min⁡{1,(ν2​k2​ln⁡TT)1/3}\delta_{t}=r\,\min\left\{1,(\tfrac{\nu^{2}{k}^{2}\ln T}{T})^{1/3}\right\} and ℬ\mathcal{B} runs P-FTRL (4) with ηn=1n​λ\eta_{n}=\tfrac{1}{n\lambda}, guarantees

R¯T​(x∗)\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*}) =O(G2λ[min{σmaxlnT,dtot}\displaystyle=O\!\left(\tfrac{G^{2}}{\lambda}\left[\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\}\right.\right.
+T2/3(lnT)1/3(νk)2/3]).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\left.\left.\,+\,T^{2/3}(\ln T)^{1/3}(\nu{k})^{2/3}\right]\right).

The proofs of both corollaries combine Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, using a concentration bound for ‖∑m=n−d~n⋆n−1g^~mδ‖\|\sum_{m=n-\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}}^{n-1}\widetilde{\widehat{g}}^{\delta}_{m}\| to control the drift term in Appendix E.

6 Skipping Scheme

The O⁡(dtot)O(\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}) term in Corollaries 5.3 and 5.7 is pessimistic when delays are highly unbalanced: if a few rounds have exceptionally large delays, it is preferable to skip them (i.e., accept full loss and ignore their feedback), improving the bound to O⁡(minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+(∑t∉Qdt)12})O(\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\{|Q|+(\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\}). For instance, following Thune et al. (2019), if the first ⌊T⌋\lfloor\,{\sqrt{T}}\,\rfloor rounds have delay Θ⁡(T)\Theta(T) and the rest have 11, we get improvement from O⁡(T3/4)O(T^{3/4}) to O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}). However, as delays are revealed upon feedback arrival, achieving this adaptively is nontrivial.

To address this, we adopt the skipping technique of Zimmert and Seldin (2020) as an external wrapper, 𝒮skip{\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}} (Algorithm 3), making it applicable to any delayed OCO algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The wrapper acts as an interface between 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the environment, maintaining a tracking set SS of rounds awaiting feedback. When feedback for s∈Ss\in S arrives, it is forwarded to 𝒜\mathcal{A}; if ss remains pending for too long, it is “skipped” by forwarding zero-valued feedback and removing ss from SS. Thus, in effect, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is presented with a different delayed OCO problem, one with shorter delays and zero losses on skipped rounds.

By construction, for every t∈[T]t\in[T], the wrapper passes feedback with index tt to 𝒜\mathcal{A} at round t+dt′t+d^{\prime}_{t} for some dt′∈{0,…,dt}d^{\prime}_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,d_{t}\}: either the true feedback (t,vt)(t,v_{t}) upon arrival or dummy feedback (t,0)(t,0) forwarded preemptively. Let Q∗⊆[T]Q^{*}\subseteq[T] denote the set of skipped rounds, i.e., those for which dummy feedback was forwarded, and define ft′=ft𝕀(t∉Q∗)f^{\prime}_{t}=f_{t}\,\ind(t\notin Q^{*}). Then, in effect, 𝒮skip{\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}} presents 𝒜\mathcal{A} with a delayed OCO problem having losses {ft′}t=1T\{f^{\prime}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} and delays {dt′}t=1T\{d^{\prime}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. The following theorem bounds the regret of 𝒮skip​(𝒜){\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}}(\mathcal{A}).

Theorem 6.1.

The regret RT​(u)R_{T}(u) of 𝒮skip​(𝒜){\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}}(\mathcal{A}) against any comparator u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K} satisfies RT​(u)≤RT′​(u)+G​D​|Q∗|R_{T}(u)\leq R^{\prime}_{T}(u)+GD|Q^{*}|, where RT′​(u)=∑t=1T(ft′​(xt)−ft′​(u))R^{\prime}_{T}(u)=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}(f^{\prime}_{t}(x_{t})-f^{\prime}_{t}(u)) is the regret of 𝒜\mathcal{A} on delayed OCO problem with losses and delays {ft′,dt′}t=1T\{f^{\prime}_{t},d^{\prime}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}. Moreover, the number of skipped rounds |Q∗||Q^{*}| and the total modified delay dtot′=∑t=1Tdt′d_{\textnormal{tot}}^{\prime}=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}d^{\prime}_{t} satisfy

|Q∗|+dtot′\displaystyle|Q^{*}|+\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}^{\prime}} =O⁡(minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+∑t∉Qdt}).\displaystyle=O\left(\textstyle\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\left\{|Q|+\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t}}\right\}\right).

Composing 𝒮skip{\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}} with wrappers 𝒲OCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}} and 𝒲BCO\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}} immediately improves upon Corollaries 5.3 and 5.7, respectively.

Corollary 6.2.

Under the conditions of Corollaries 5.3 and 5.7, applying the skipping wrapper yields:

RT​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​[minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+∑t∉Qdt}+T]),\displaystyle R_{T}(x^{*})=O\bigg(\!GD\bigg[\!\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\Big\{\!|Q|\!+\!\sqrt{\!\textstyle\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t}\!}\Big\}\!+\!\sqrt{T}\bigg]\!\bigg),
R¯T​(x∗)=O⁡(G​D​[minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+∑t∉Qdt}+T34​ν​k]),\displaystyle\widebar{R}_{T}(x^{*})=O\bigg(\!GD\bigg[\!\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\Big\{\!|Q|\!+\!\sqrt{\!\textstyle\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t}\!}\Big\}\!+\!T^{\frac{3}{4}}\sqrt{\!\nu k}\bigg]\!\bigg),

for 𝒮skip​(𝒲OCO​(ℬ)){\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}}(\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{OCO}}(\mathcal{B})) and 𝒮skip​(𝒲BCO​(ℬ)){\mathcal{S}}_{\textnormal{skip}}(\mathcal{W}_{\textnormal{BCO}}(\mathcal{B})), respectively.

The proofs are deferred to Appendix F.

This skipping scheme applies in any setting where a zero loss is admissible, e.g., the general convex case. In the strongly convex case, one could instead skip rounds by substituting λ2​x2\frac{\lambda}{2}x^{2} loss values. However, minQ⊆[T]⁡{|Q|+(∑t∉Qdt)1/2}=Ω⁡(σmax)\min_{Q\subseteq[T]}\{|Q|+(\sum_{t\notin Q}d_{t})^{1/2}\}=\Omega(\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}) as shown by Qiu et al. (2025), so our strongly convex bound O⁡(min⁡{σmax​ln⁡T,dtot})O(\min\{\sigma_{\textnormal{max}}\ln T,\sqrt{d_{\textnormal{tot}}}\}) already matches this benchmark up to a ln⁡T\ln T factor.

7 Discussion and Future Work

We introduced a continuous-time model for online learning with delayed feedback that places prediction and observation events on a single timeline. This observation-centric viewpoint leads to a black-box reduction to drift-penalized online linear optimization: wrapping any base algorithm with regret and stability guarantees yields a delayed learner whose regret is controlled by the base algorithm’s drift-penalized regret under the induced observation ordering.

Crucially, our continuous-time model provides a general framework for delayed feedback that extends beyond the specific scope of online convex optimization. It offers a modular template for handling delays in any online learning protocol where prediction stability and drift can be quantified, and we expect the reduction to be useful beyond the settings studied here.

Several directions remain open. First, our analysis assumes an oblivious adversary that fixes losses and delays in advance. Extending the framework to adaptive adversaries, where delays may depend on the learner’s actions, would be technically challenging and is relevant to congestion control and strategic environments. Second, delayed feedback is pervasive in distributed optimization with asynchronous communication. Our model may provide a useful abstraction for multi-agent online learning with heterogeneous, time-varying delays, including federated learning systems.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

Online convex optimization.

Online convex optimization (OCO) and its feedback models have been studied extensively. Early work includes Zinkevich (2003), who introduced online convex programming and established O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T})-type guarantees for online gradient methods. For first-order feedback, subsequent work established the standard Θ⁡(T)\Theta(\sqrt{T}) minimax scaling for general convex losses (see, e.g., Abernethy et al., 2008). For λ\lambda-strongly convex losses, logarithmic regret is achievable; in particular, Hazan et al. (2007) gives O⁡(ln⁡T)O(\ln T)-type guarantees (matching the Ω⁡(ln⁡T)\Omega(\ln T) lower bound of Abernethy et al., 2008). Background and further developments can be found in Hazan and others (2016); Orabona (2019).

Bandit convex optimization.

Bandit convex optimization (BCO) was initiated by Flaxman et al. (2004), who introduced the classical single-point gradient estimator and obtained regret of order O⁡(T3/4​k1/2)O(T^{3/4}k^{1/2}). Subsequently, Agarwal et al. (2010) developed optimal algorithms for multi-point bandit feedback and sharpened guarantees: in particular, for two-point feedback they obtain O~​(T1/2​k2)\widetilde{O}(T^{1/2}k^{2}) regret for convex losses and O⁡(k2​ln⁡T)O(k^{2}\ln T) regret under strong convexity; for single-point feedback, they also note improved rates under additional curvature, including a T2/3T^{2/3}-type guarantee for strongly convex losses (more precisely, O⁡((T2​ln⁡T)1/3​k2/3)O((T^{2}\ln T)^{1/3}k^{2/3}) up to problem-dependent constants). Complementary results for stochastic convex optimization under bandit feedback appear in Agarwal et al. (2011). For two-point feedback, Shamir (2017) gives an optimal algorithm with improved dimension dependence with regret O⁡(T1/2​k1/2)O(T^{1/2}k^{1/2}). A line of work designs (nearly) minimax-optimal algorithms for general BCO, approaching the Ω⁡(k​T)\Omega(k\sqrt{T}) lower bound of Shamir (2013); see, e.g., Bubeck and Eldan (2016); Hazan and Li (2016); Lattimore (2020). These methods typically incur prohibitive computational costs (exponential or high-degree polynomial dependence on kk and/or TT), and we refer to Lattimore (2024) for a detailed treatment and further references.

Online convex optimization with delayed feedback.

Early work on online learning with delayed feedback includes Weinberger and Ordentlich (2002). A systematic treatment of delayed-feedback online learning and reduction-style approaches appears in Joulani et al. (2013), and Joulani et al. (2016) develops a black-box-style reduction that processes feedback in order of arrival. Beyond black-box techniques, there is substantial work on algorithms tailored to delayed OCO (e.g., Langford et al., 2009; McMahan and Streeter, 2014; Quanrud and Khashabi, 2015; Flaspohler et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025). Delayed BCO has also received focused attention, starting from delayed extensions of bandit gradient methods (Héliou et al., 2020) and followed by delay-adaptive or improved-delay-dependence results (Bistritz et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2024).

Delays in related sequential decision problems.

Delayed observations have been studied extensively in multi-armed bandits and related models (see, e.g., Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2016; Thune et al., 2019; Bistritz et al., 2022; Esposito et al., 2023; Masoudian et al., 2022; Masoudian et al., 2024). Delays also arise naturally under resource limitations such as capacity constraints (Ryabchenko et al., 2025). Delayed feedback has also been studied in adversarial contextual bandits with general function approximation (Levy et al., 2025). Delays also appear in reinforcement learning / MDP settings with delayed or asynchronous feedback (e.g., Bouteiller et al., 2020; Lancewicki et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2022; van der Hoeven et al., 2023).

Fact B.1.

Under Assumptions 2.2 and 2.3, the diameter of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is bounded by 2​Gλ\frac{2G}{\lambda}, i.e., supx,y∈𝒦‖x−y‖≤2​Gλ\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{K}}\left\|x-y\right\|\leq\frac{2G}{\lambda}.

Hence, supx,y∈𝒦‖x−y‖≤2​Gλ<∞\sup_{x,y\in\mathcal{K}}\left\|x-y\right\|\leq\frac{2G}{\lambda}<\infty. ∎

For every choice of N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, real numbers x1≤x2≤…≤xNx_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq...\leq x_{N}, y1≤y2≤…≤yNy_{1}\leq y_{2}\leq...\leq y_{N}, and index permutation ρ:[N]→[N]\rho:[N]\to[N], it holds that

x1​yN+…+xN​y1≤x1​yρ⁡(1)+…​xN​yρ⁡(N)≤x1​y1+…+xN​yN.\displaystyle x_{1}y_{N}+...+x_{N}y_{1}\leq x_{1}y_{\rho(1)}+...x_{N}y_{\rho(N)}\leq x_{1}y_{1}+...+x_{N}y_{N}.
Proof.

This fact restates Theorem 368 in Hardy (1952). ∎

Fact B.4 (Square-Root Telescoping Inequality).

Let (Xn)n≥1(X_{n})_{n\geq 1} be non-negative reals and X1>0X_{1}>0.

Appendix C Technical Results for the Continuous Time Model: Proofs

This section establishes the technical results concerning the CTM (Definition 3.1). Recall the observation-ordering convention (Definition 3.5): a~n=aρ⁡(n)\widetilde{\mathrm{a}}_{n}=\mathrm{a}_{\rho(n)}, where ρ\rho is the permutation of [T][T] satisfying rρ⁡(1)≤⋯≤rρ⁡(T)r_{\rho(1)}\leq\cdots\leq r_{\rho(T)}. Fact C.1 serves as a central tool throughout this section, connecting delays and backlogs with their duals. Facts C.2 and C.3 are used in the proof of Corollary 5.7, while Fact C.4 plays a key role in the analysis of delay-adaptive learning rates.

Fact C.1.

Define β⁡(t)=|{s:rs≤rt}|\beta(t)=|\{s:r_{s}\leq r_{t}\}|. For all t∈[T]t\in[T], σt⋆=dt+t−β⁡(t)\sigma^{\star}_{t}=d_{t}+t-\beta(t) and dt⋆=σt+β⁡(t)−td^{\star}_{t}=\sigma_{t}+\beta(t)-t. Furthermore, β=ρ−1\beta=\rho^{-1} as permutations of [T][T], and for all n∈[T]n\in[T], σ~n⋆=d~n+ρ⁡(n)−n\widetilde{\sigma}^{\star}_{n}=\widetilde{d}_{n}+\rho(n)-n and d~n⋆=σ~n+n−ρ⁡(n)\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{n}=\widetilde{\sigma}_{n}+n-\rho(n).

Proof.

t+dt\displaystyle t+d_{t} =|{s:ls<rt}|=|{s:rs≤rt}|+|{s:ls<rt<rs}|=β⁡(t)+σt⋆,\displaystyle=|\{s:l_{s}<r_{t}\}|=|\{s:r_{s}\leq r_{t}\}|+|\{s:l_{s}<r_{t}<r_{s}\}|=\beta(t)+\sigma^{\star}_{t},
t−σt\displaystyle t-\sigma_{t} =|{s:rs<lt}∪{t}|=|{s:rs≤rt}|−|{s:lt<rs<rt}|=β⁡(t)−dt⋆.\displaystyle=|\{s:r_{s}<l_{t}\}\cup\{t\}|=|\{s:r_{s}\leq r_{t}\}|-|\{s:l_{t}<r_{s}<r_{t}\}|=\beta(t)-d^{\star}_{t}.

The remaining identities follow by substituting t=ρ⁡(n)t=\rho(n). ∎

Theorem 3.4 (Restated).

For quantities in (1) and (2), it holds that:

    n2≥∑m=1nm≥∑m=1n(d~m⋆+1)≥1+∑m=1nd~m⋆.n^{2}\geq\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{n}m\geq\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{n}(\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}+1)\geq 1+\textstyle\sum_{m=1}^{n}\widetilde{d}^{\star}_{m}.
